I confess I was short with him. I believed, as widows are inclined to believe, that every hand in the press room of Port of Spain was waiting to carry off some piece of my husband's trade. items.passage: Three times Tendai invited me to supper, and three times I refused, each time with a reason that sounded better on the stair than it had in my head. We shared a wall, Tendai and I, in a narrow house near the Company's Garden, and through that wall I heard her sing while she cooked, badly and with great happiness. I told myself I was too busy. In truth I was a widow of one year, and a table set for two seemed to me a kind of trap. I took to spending evenings in the reading room of the public library, where silence was not only allowed but required. One night I looked up from my book and saw Tendai at the next table, reading a cookery manual with a pencil behind her ear. She did not invite me again. She only slid a slip of paper across the table: a list of dishes, with a question mark beside each. I have kept it, though I am ashamed to say how long I took to answer. The reading lamps in that room were green, and they hummed when the trams went by.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator Sunethra's attitude in the text?
options: Lingering resentment of Tendai for intruding on her private grief
Rueful self-awareness about her refusals and fondness for Tendai
Amused contempt for Tendai's poor singing and clumsy cooking
Proud satisfaction at having protected her solitude successfully

items.passage: Folasade read the last of their mother's letters aloud while Obinna sat by the guesthouse window, where the monks' bell rope hung motionless in the noon heat of Dakar. The plan had succeeded: the house in Lagos was sold, the debts were paid, and their mother would join them before the rains. Every letter said she was grateful. Not one said she was glad. Between the final pages Folasade found a pressed hibiscus, faded to the color of weak tea, which their mother had always picked from the vine beside the old front door. Obinna turned it over in his palm and remarked that the new house had no such vine. "We can plant one," Folasade said. He laid the flower on the windowsill, and neither of them moved to return it to the envelope, though the breeze kept nudging it toward the edge.

the quiet routine of the monks that the siblings hope to imitate.
the new house that the mother will soon share with her children.
the attachment to home that the mother gave up for the siblings' plan.

items.passage: Astrid did not believe in new gates. For forty years she had repaired the oak gate of the cemetery in Bergen, replacing one rotten slat at a time, so that by now hardly a board of the original remained. Her apprentice, Anahera, wanted to mark the gate's hundredth year with something grand: a carved arch, the town's name in gold leaf. Astrid only handed her a plane and a single slat cut from the same stand of oak. "One board," she said. "Each year, one board." Anahera fitted it beside a slat that Astrid's own teacher had set, and the grain of the two ran nearly together. That evening the gate swung shut behind the last mourners, and the hinges, oiled that morning, made no sound at all.
items.question: In the text, the cemetery gate most likely symbolizes
options: a tradition kept alive through small renewals passed between generations.
the private grief of the mourners who visit the cemetery every evening.
Anahera's desire to bring bold and visible changes to the old town.
the gradual decline of careful craftsmanship in a modernizing city.
